passages.happening:
In the fifth month of Zedekiah's fourth year, the prophet Hananiah son of Azzur, from Gibeon, speaks to Jeremiah in the temple before the priests and all the people (verse 1). He says in the LORD's name that God has broken the yoke of the king of Babylon (verse 2). Within two years God will bring back the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar took (verse 3), and King Jeconiah and all the exiles (verse 4).

Jeremiah answers before them all. Amen, he says; may the LORD do it, and bring back the vessels and the exiles (verse 6). But listen (verse 7): the prophets before them prophesied war, disaster and plague against many lands (verse 8). ‘As for the prophet who prophesies peace, only if the word of the prophet comes true will the prophet be recognized as one the LORD has truly sent’ (verse 9).

Then Hananiah takes the yoke off Jeremiah's neck and breaks it (verse 10). Before all the people he says that in the same way, within two years, God will break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar from the neck of all the nations. And Jeremiah goes on his way (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The date is the summer of 594 or 593 BC, a few years after the first deportation and in the same year as the envoys' meeting of chapter 27. Jeconiah, or Jehoiachin, was still alive in Babylon, and many in Judah still saw him as the true king.

Hananiah came from Gibeon, a town a few miles northwest of Jerusalem assigned to the priests. Nothing else is known of him. He used the very words true prophets used: thus says the LORD. His message drew on real promises. Isaiah had spoken of God breaking the oppressor's yoke, and in Hezekiah's day God had saved Jerusalem.

Jeremiah's answer is striking. He does not mock Hananiah. He says Amen and wishes it were true. Then he points to the test of time: a prophet of peace is proved only when the peace comes. And when Hananiah breaks the yoke, Jeremiah simply walks away.
passages.later: The law gave the test Jeremiah used: a word that ‘does not come to pass or come true’ is not from the LORD (Deuteronomy 18:22). Micaiah said the same to King Ahab: ‘If you ever return safely, the LORD has not spoken through me’ (1 Kings 22:28).
passages.asks: Jeremiah wished Hananiah were right and still would not pretend he was. Ask whether you can hope for good news while refusing to believe a lie. And ask what you do when someone publicly breaks what you have said: argue, or walk away and wait on God.

passages.t: A yoke of iron, and Hananiah's death
passages.happening:
Some time after Hananiah broke the yoke, the word of the LORD comes to Jeremiah (verse 12). He is to tell Hananiah, ‘You have broken a yoke of wood, but in its place you have fashioned a yoke of iron’ (verse 13). God has put an iron yoke on the necks of all these nations to serve Nebuchadnezzar, and even the wild animals (verse 14).

Jeremiah says to Hananiah, “Listen, Hananiah! The LORD did not send you, but you have persuaded this people to trust in a lie” (verse 15). So God will remove him from the face of the earth. He will die this year, because he has preached rebellion against the LORD (verse 16).

‘And in the seventh month of that very year, the prophet Hananiah died’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Wood can be broken. Iron cannot. Hananiah's show of breaking the yoke only made the coming bondage harder, because it encouraged a rebellion that would bring Babylon's full force on Jerusalem.

The law of Deuteronomy set death as the penalty for a prophet who presumed to speak what God had not commanded. Here God carries out the sentence himself, not a mob. Two months later Hananiah was dead. His two years became two months.

The chapter does not tell Hananiah's motives. He may well have believed what he said. But speaking in God's name is serious, because others build their lives on it. He made the people trust in a lie.
passages.later: The law said, ‘if any prophet dares to speak a message in My name that I have not commanded him to speak’, he must die (Deuteronomy 18:20). James warns, ‘Not many of you should become teachers’ (James 3:1).
passages.hard:
Hananiah may have sincerely believed what he said. Why was his death a fair judgment?

The chapter does not give his motives, and he may well have believed he spoke for God. His message drew on real promises. But the Bible treats speaking in God's name as a sober responsibility with real effects on others: Hananiah made the people trust in a lie (verse 15), which fed the rebellion that brought Jerusalem's destruction. The law of Deuteronomy 13 and 18 set death as the penalty for a prophet who presumed to speak what God had not commanded, and here God carries out that sentence himself.

Readers who find this severe should notice that Jeremiah does not gloat. He hoped to be wrong (verse 6), walked away from the confrontation (verse 11), and spoke the judgment only when God sent him back. The story gives no one a warrant to harm anyone they judge a false teacher.
passages.asks: Hananiah's words gave people false hope and led them to ruin. Ask how carefully you speak when you tell others what God will do. And ask whether you have trusted a comforting lie because it promised a quick end to hardship.
